stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the signing of the Social Security Amendments of 1965, July 30, 1965, in Independence, Missouri. President Lyndon Johnson signed the law creating Medicare, health insurance for Americans 65 and older, and Medicaid, medical coverage for Americans who could not afford their own insurance. Former President Harry S. Truman, then 81 years old, sat beside Johnson and received the first Medicare card as the program's first beneficiary. When Medicare services began on July 1, 1966, more than 19 million Americans 65 and older had enrolled.

stem: Johnson's choice of Truman as the first Medicare beneficiary most directly shows which of the following?

options.text: Truman was the oldest person living in Missouri in 1965
options.misconception: The passage gives Truman's age as 81, but it does not say he was the oldest person in Missouri.

options.text: Johnson wanted to thank Truman for winning the Korean War
options.misconception: The passage links Truman to the new health program, not to the Korean War.

options.text: Medicare completed an idea Truman had pushed twenty years earlier
Truman had written the Medicare law himself in 1965
options.misconception: The passage says Johnson signed the law in 1965; Truman was a guest at the signing, not its author.

rationales.A: The passage gives Truman's age as 81, but it does not say he was the oldest person in Missouri.
rationales.B: The passage links Truman to the new health program, not to the Korean War.
rationales.C: Background: Truman had proposed national health insurance in 1945, twenty years before Johnson signed Medicare into law.
rationales.D: The passage says Johnson signed the law in 1965; Truman was a guest at the signing, not its author.
rationales.general:
1. Johnson did not give the first card to a stranger; he gave it to a former president.
2. Background: Truman had proposed national health insurance in 1945, twenty years before this signing.
3. The ceremony therefore linked the new law to an old fight.
4. The first card honored Truman as the one who had pushed the idea first.
Remember: A ceremony's guest of honor often points to the idea's history.
